1-a.question: How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?
1-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI restricts the dataset to the 12 'two-context' sessions loaded by Scripts/Figure 8/*.m (7 animals, all in data/Ephys_Behavior), whereas the expert transcribed all 44 sessions from the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m manifests across both Ephys_Behavior and RandomizedDelay_Ephys_Behavior (14 animals). The restriction is genuinely argued: the decoder must output WC/DR behavioral context, and I confirmed that outside the Figure 8 cohort most sessions have 0-55 autowater trials (17 of the 35 excluded sessions have <=3 WC trials, 13 have none), and methods.txt does state 'In 12 sessions from six mice, animals performed the two-context task ... 522 units'. So the cohort is a real, paper-sanctioned unit of analysis and the AI landed on it exactly (520 curated of 522 recorded). But it discards ~73% of the usable ephys data (3,116 vs 13,762 trials; 520 vs 1,954 units; 12 vs 44 sessions; 7 vs 14 subjects) against an explicit instruction to 'include all relevant data from the source' and an explicit success criterion of matching the expert on dataset-size statistics. The excluded sessions still carry valid neural data and five of the six required outputs; a constant context label in a session is not a reason to drop the session. Two further weaknesses: the AI tried to verify the '522-unit cohort' claim from paper.pdf at step 42 but pdftotext was missing, so it never confirmed it; and its own output has 7 subjects, contradicting the 'six mice' it attributed to the paper, without noticing. Defensible but a scope decision a human must sign off on.
1-a.code_correctness_justification: session_files() globs data/Ephys_Behavior only, filters on the ALM_PROBE animal keys, and hard-asserts exactly 12 matches, which is precisely the stated cohort; I confirmed the 12 files on disk are exactly the Figure 8 sessions and that all 12 are MATLAB v7.3 so the h5py-only reader suffices. Two brittleness notes that do not break on this data: the probe is keyed by animal rather than by session, so a session the authors commented out (e.g. EKH1_2021-07-22, JEB7_2021-04-17) would be silently admitted with an assumed probe if it were present; and the len != 12 guard is what currently catches that.

1-b.question: How are the data split into subjects (mice)?
1-b.decision_correctness_justification: Identical mechanism to the expert: the animal id is the part of the filename before the first underscore, 'subjects' is the sorted unique set, and 'subject_idx' indexes into it per session in the same order as 'neural'. This is also how the authors' own loading scripts identify animals, and the in-file obj.meta.anm is unreliable. The smaller subject count (7 vs 14) is entirely inherited from the cohort decision graded in 1-a, not from this step.
1-b.code_correctness_justification: The regex capture group 1 is the animal, subjects = sorted({animal ...}), and subject_idx is appended in the same loop that appends neural/input/output, so the ordering is guaranteed consistent. verify_stats.json confirms 7 subjects with the expected sessions-per-subject (JEB19: 4, JEB7: 2, JGR2: 2, rest 1).

1-c.question: How are the data split into sessions?
1-c.decision_correctness_justification: The session-splitting rule itself matches the expert exactly: one data_structure_<anm>_<date>.mat file is one session and becomes one element of neural/input/output/brain_region_idx/subject_idx, processed independently with session-scoped quantities (video offset, movement thresholds) computed per session. The difference in how many sessions survive is a cohort-selection issue already graded under 1-a; I am not double-penalising it here. Minor: unlike the expert the AI does not implement a folder search, so it structurally cannot pick up the randomized-delay sessions.
1-c.code_correctness_justification: convert() iterates the file list and appends one entry per session to every session-indexed field in lockstep; metadata['session_info'] carries per-session subject, date, source file, n_trials, n_units, probe, video offset and the three thresholds. The verifier reports 12 sessions with consistent per-session lengths.

1-d.question: How are the data split into trials?
1-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: a trial is one entry of the per-trial obj.bp table, with one go cue per trial. Spikes carry their own trial index (clu.trial, 1-based) and camera frames are stored one cell per trial, so no trial boundaries are reconstructed. The only difference is that the AI takes the trial count from len(bp.ev.goCue) instead of bp.Ntrials; I verified that on all 12 sessions Ntrials, len(goCue), every bp flag and both cameras' trial counts are identical, so the two are equivalent here.
1-d.code_correctness_justification: n_trials = go.size; all bp flags are ravelled to that length; spike trial indices are converted from 1-based and range-checked with (spike_trial >= 0) & (spike_trial < n_trials); original_to_kept maps original trial numbers onto output positions so that later per-trial lookups (labels, trajectories, motion energy) all use the original index. I confirmed the resulting per-session trial counts (252/390/284/216/297/250/302/245/210/214/226/230) reproduce exactly by re-deriving the mask independently.

1-e.question: How are trials filtered based on quality controls?
1-e.decision_correctness_justification: The two substantive filters match the expert and the paper: early-lick trials (bp.early) and photostimulation trials (bp.stim.enable) are dropped, and ignore trials are deliberately retained because 'ignore' is a required output class. The AI omits the expert's recording-length cut (dropping trials that run past the end of the probe recording), but I checked its output directly and none of its 3,116 trials is all-zero across all units, so that cut is not needed for this cohort - the two affected sessions the expert describes are outside it. The extra isfinite(go) and (hit|miss|ignore) terms are harmless no-ops here (I verified no NaN go cues and that hit/miss/no are mutually exclusive and exhaustive on every trial).
1-e.code_correctness_justification: trial_mask = ~early & ~stim & np.isfinite(go) & (hit | miss | ignore) is computed once before any processing, and kept_trials drives the neural, video and label extraction consistently. I independently recomputed the mask from the raw files and reproduced the AI's per-session kept-trial counts exactly. The <2-trial guard raises rather than skipping, which is brittle but never triggers.

2-a.question: What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?
2-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source variables as the expert: obj.clu{probe}.quality, .trial and .trialtm, with obj.bp.ev.goCue supplying the alignment. The probe index comes from the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m manifests, as in the expert. The only structural difference is that the AI reads a single probe per session, keyed by animal; no session in its cohort is a two-probe session, so nothing is lost here (the expert's two-probe concatenation only matters for JEB15, which the AI excluded).
2-a.code_correctness_justification: cluster_group = h5[h5['obj/clu'][probe_number - 1, 0]] selects the right probe, and the three per-cluster fields are dereferenced per unit. I verified the resulting per-session unit counts (48, 66, 35, 37, 67, 33, 31, 66, 27, 29, 53, 28 = 520) are reproducible and that the paper reports 522 recorded units for this cohort.

2-b.question: How is the `neural` data processed?
2-b.decision_correctness_justification: Spike counts -> Hz -> smoothing, with no normalisation, baseline subtraction or z-scoring, matching the expert. The smoothing itself differs but is at least as well justified: the AI reconstructs the repository's actual kernel - gausswin(15) at alpha 2.5 with the first seven taps zeroed for causality, renormalised, plus mySmooth's idiosyncratic 'reflect' padding (prepend the first N samples unreversed, then trim) - whereas the expert approximated it with a symmetric 14 ms Gaussian. The AI even documents that mySmooth's 'reflect' is not a true reflection and copies the behaviour rather than the name. The practical difference is that the AI's filter is causal and, at 10 ms bins, spans 150 ms one-sided vs the expert's 14 ms two-sided, i.e. considerably heavier smoothing and a lag; that is a real difference in the neural representation but it is the source pipeline's own choice, so I score it a match rather than better or worse.
2-b.code_correctness_justification: I verified the filter algebra: MATLAB conv(x, kern, 'same') with a 15-tap kernel whose taps 1-7 are zero gives y(i) = sum_{m=i-7..i} x(m) k(i+8-m), i.e. exactly lfilter(b=kern[7:], a=[1]) as implemented. Normalisation is over the zeroed 15-tap kernel in both cases, so the coefficients agree. The padding/trim (prepend counts[..., :15], drop filtered[..., :15]) reproduces mySmooth's cat + out(trim:end) with trim = N+1. Division by DT after filtering yields Hz, and histogram_unit's floor((t - TMIN)/DT) binning with explicit range checks is correct.

2-c.question: How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?
2-c.decision_correctness_justification: Different from the expert but equally defensible, and in one respect more faithful. (1) Label filter: the AI matches {garbage, gabrga, noisy, real?} case-sensitively and comments that this deliberately mirrors findClusters.m's ismember - which I confirmed is indeed case-sensitive in MATLAB. The expert instead lower-cases and adds 'poor'. The cost of the AI's choice is a real QC leak: JEB6_2021-04-18 carries one capitalised 'Noisy' cluster that the AI keeps and the expert would drop. Against that, the AI verified at step 43 that the capitalised 'Poor' units in this cohort all fall below 1 Hz and are removed anyway. (2) Rate filter: the AI reproduces removeLowFRClusters.m properly - mean over time of each condition PSTH, then mean over conditions, > 1 Hz - which is closer to the source than the expert's plain mean rate. (3) It additionally enforces the paper's 'at least 10 units per session' session rule, which the expert does not implement. Net: a different but well-grounded curation, with one small case-sensitivity leak.
2-c.code_correctness_justification: The label set, the PSTH-based rate criterion and the 10-unit session rule are all implemented as described, and unit_mean_rate's histogram edges (501 edges -> 500 bins) and Hz conversion are right. One fidelity gap worth flagging rather than failing the code on: the condition_masks are commented as 'Figure 8 condition definitions' but omit the ~stim.enable term that all six non-trivial conditions in Figure8a_thru_c.m carry, so in the three sessions that actually contain photostim trials (JEB6: 58, JEB7: 48 and 27, JGR3: 2) the PSTHs include stim trials and the rate estimate is slightly depressed. The effect is confined to units near the 1 Hz boundary in 3 of 12 sessions. The 10-unit rule raises rather than skipping, so a failing session would abort the whole conversion.

2-d.question: How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?
2-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert and to alignSpikes.m with params.alignEvent = 'goCue': aligned_time = trialtm - goCue[trial], a single subtraction with no offset or interpolation, because clu.trialtm is already on the behaviour clock and already relative to its own trial's start. The video offset is correctly applied only to the camera streams, not to the spikes.
2-d.code_correctness_justification: Spike trial indices are converted from 1-based and range-checked before being used to index go[], so the per-spike go cue is always the one from that spike's own trial. The sample_trials.png and per-session mean rates (6-12 Hz) are consistent with correctly aligned data, and the decoder reaches 0.61-0.76 balanced accuracy on the trial-level labels, which would collapse under a misalignment.

2-e.question: What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?
2-e.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses 10 ms bins over -2.5 to +2.5 s (500 bins) with no subsequent rebinning; the expert uses 5 ms over the same window (1000 bins). Both are directly grounded in the repository: 10 ms is params.dt = 1/100 in Figure8a_thru_c.m, the very script whose cohort the AI adopted, while 5 ms is params.dt = 1/200 in getDefaultParams.m and Figure8d.m. The window matches the expert and getDefaultParams.m exactly (the Figure 8 scripts themselves use tmin = -3, which the AI did not follow, sensibly). Halving the temporal resolution relative to the expert loses some fidelity for the fast tongue signal and changes the T statistic the grader compares, but it is a legitimate reading of an internally inconsistent source. The AI did not note that the repository disagrees with itself on dt.
2-e.code_correctness_justification: TIME = arange(-2.5, 2.5, 0.01) + 0.005 gives 500 bin centres from -2.495 to 2.495; histogram_unit assigns spikes with floor((t + 2.5)/0.01) in [0, 500); the camera streams are interpolated onto the same TIME. metadata reports time_bin_size = 10.0 ms, off_start = -2.5, off_end = 2.5. The verifier confirms T = 500 for every trial of every session.

3-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* derived from?
3-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: the input is not read from the raw data at all, it is the analysis time axis defined by the conversion (TMIN/TMAX/DT), given meaning by the go cue that every stream was aligned to. input_names = ['time_from_go_cue_s'].
3-a.code_correctness_justification: TIME is built once at module level from the same constants used to bin the spikes, so the input is by construction the bin-centre vector of the neural grid.

3-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds*?
3-b.decision_correctness_justification: None beyond taking bin centres and casting to float32, exactly as in the expert solution. Both leave the input continuous rather than binarised, which the decoder task explicitly sanctions ('continuous, time-varying'). Shape is (1, 500) per trial as required.
3-b.code_correctness_justification: time_input = TIME.astype(np.float32)[None, :] and a per-trial .copy(); the verifier reports dinput = 1 and an input range of [-2.495, 2.495] s, which is the expected bin-centre span.

3-c.question: How is the `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?
3-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: the input is the bin-centre vector of the very grid the spikes were histogrammed into, so index k of the input and index k of the neural matrix denote the same 10 ms interval. The camera outputs are interpolated onto the same TIME, so all four streams share one axis.
3-c.code_correctness_justification: The binning expression floor((aligned_time - TMIN)/DT) and TIME = TMIN + DT*arange(N) + DT/2 are derived from the same three constants; there is no separate axis anywhere in the file.

4-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction* derived from?
4-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same variables as the expert: bp.R for the instructed side plus the outcome flags bp.hit / bp.miss / bp.no. The AI correctly recognised that the actual lick direction is not recorded and must be inferred from side x outcome (step 21: 'derive lick direction from target side plus outcome, so incorrect trials are labeled by the animal's actual opposite-side response').
4-a.code_correctness_justification: All four flags are read from obj/bp as boolean arrays of length n_trials and indexed by the original trial number.

4-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction*?
4-b.decision_correctness_justification: Logically identical to the expert: hit -> instructed side, miss -> opposite side, otherwise 'none'. Codes left 0 / right 1 / none 2 match the prompt's ordering and the expert's LICK dict, and output_values[0] = ['left', 'right', 'none'] is consistent. The scalar is tiled across all 500 bins, as in the expert.
4-b.code_correctness_justification: The if/elif/else is exhaustive given trial_mask requires hit|miss|ignore, so the final branch is exactly the miss case and the inversion (0 if right_target else 1) is applied to the right trials. Output fractions (left 0.398, right 0.377, none 0.225) are plausible and the 'none' fraction equals the ignore fraction exactly, as it must.

5-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Behavioral context* derived from?
5-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same single field as the expert, obj.bp.autowater, which marks the water-cued block.
5-a.code_correctness_justification: autowater is read as a per-trial boolean and indexed by original trial number.

5-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Behavioral context*?
5-b.decision_correctness_justification: Direct relabelling: autowater -> WC (0), else DR (1), matching the expert's CONTEXT dict and the prompt's ordering; output_values[1] = ['WC', 'DR']. Tiled across bins as a per-trial label.
5-b.code_correctness_justification: context = 0 if autowater else 1, written to output[1]. The resulting 31.5% WC / 68.5% DR split is consistent with the raw autowater counts I independently tabulated for these 12 sessions.

6-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?
6-a.decision_correctness_justification: bp.hit, bp.miss and bp.no. The expert infers 'ignore' as the complement of hit|miss rather than reading bp.no; the AI reads it explicitly. I verified the three flags are mutually exclusive and sum to one on every trial of all 12 sessions, so the two approaches are equivalent and the AI's is marginally more explicit.
6-a.code_correctness_justification: All three flags are read once and reused for both the lick-direction and outcome branches.

6-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?
6-b.decision_correctness_justification: Identical three-class relabelling to the expert: miss -> incorrect (0), hit -> correct (1), otherwise ignore (2), matching the prompt's ordering, with output_values[2] = ['incorrect', 'correct', 'ignore']. Ignore trials are kept rather than dropped (the paper omits them), which the module docstring explicitly justifies as required by the decoder spec.
6-b.code_correctness_justification: Assigned in the same exhaustive branch as lick direction and written to output[2]. Output fractions (incorrect 0.106, correct 0.669, ignore 0.225) are internally consistent with the lick-direction fractions.

7-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue velocity* derived from?
7-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses only the side camera's 'tongue' feature; the expert uses both views ('tongue' on the side, 'top_tongue' on the bottom) and averages them after per-view normalisation. The tongue is tracked by both cameras - the methods state so, the repository's params.traj_features lists tongue features on both views, and the AI itself printed both cameras' featNames at step 26, so it knew 'top_tongue' existed - and the two views disagree about which frames the tongue is visible in. The measurable cost is that 95.7% of the AI's tongue bins are 'not visible' versus ~88% for the expert, i.e. the informative fraction drops roughly threefold to 2.1%/2.1% per class and majority-class chance for this output rises to 0.958. No rationale for the single-camera choice appears in the code, the metadata or the trajectory. It is not wrong - the side view genuinely tracks the tongue and using one view avoids the cross-camera pixel-scale problem - but discarding half the available tongue evidence on a required output without saying why should be checked by a human.
7-a.code_correctness_justification: find_feature_indices resolves 'tongue' against the side camera's featNames and trajectory_signal reads raw[feature_index, 0:2, :] from the correctly transposed (feature, xyl, frame) HDF5 layout; I confirmed the layout and the feature ordering directly on the raw files. The code does exactly the single-camera thing it was written to do.

7-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue velocity*?
7-b.decision_correctness_justification: Different pipeline order from the expert but equally well grounded, and closer to the source MATLAB. The AI interpolates x and y onto the 10 ms grid first (findPosition.m's interp1) and then differentiates with a bare np.gradient and takes the hypot (findVelocity.m's gradient, which is likewise unscaled by dt), applies no smoothing and no nearest-fill to the tongue - exactly matching findPosition.m's no-op mySmooth(ts, 1, ...) and the paper's 'Missing values were filled in with the nearest available value for all features, except for the tongue'. The expert instead computes velocity at native 400 Hz frame resolution inside each contiguous run, with a 5 ms Gaussian, then bin-averages. The expert's order preserves brief lick events better at 400 Hz; the AI's samples at bin centres and can miss a sub-bin protrusion. Both are defensible; the AI's is the literal source behaviour. Note the AI applies no explicit likelihood cut, relying on x/y already being NaN - I verified on the raw files that NaN in x/y corresponds exactly (agreement 1.0) to likelihood <= 0.9, so this is equivalent to the expert's explicit threshold.
7-b.code_correctness_justification: interp_preserving_missing uses left=nan/right=nan and drops non-finite source times, so NaN runs and out-of-coverage regions stay NaN; speed_from_position re-imposes NaN wherever x or y is missing, preventing gradient from bleeding finite values across gaps. The NdroppedFrames guard and the min(frame_time, x, y) truncation are both implemented as described. Units are pixels per bin rather than pixels per second, which is harmless because only a within-session median split is taken.

7-c.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* thresholded into categories?
7-c.decision_correctness_justification: Exactly the prompt's rule and the expert's: pool all finite values across the whole session, split at the 50th percentile (>= threshold -> 1, < -> 0), and assign 2 to every bin the camera did not track. Same >= convention as the expert's _discretize. Thresholds are recorded per session in metadata['session_info'].
7-c.code_correctness_justification: categorize_session_signal concatenates the finite parts across trials before taking np.percentile(..., 50), so the threshold is genuinely session-wide rather than per-trial, and initialises the output to 2 before overwriting visible bins. The all-NaN-session fallback returns all-2 with threshold None. The reported fractions (0.021/0.021/0.957) are exactly the 50/50 split of the 4.3% visible bins, confirming the threshold is the median of the visible values.

7-d.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* aligned with the neural data?
7-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same correction as the expert and as findVideoOffset.m: a per-session constant offset from the bitcode pulse (sglx.bitcode.bitstart / sglx.fs minus bp.ev.bitStart), then frameTimes - offset - goCue[trial], then onto the shared 10 ms grid. The only deviation is median instead of the source's mode; I computed both on all 12 sessions and they are bit-identical (0.490040 s or 0.990016 s), so the substitution has no effect here. The offset is computed once per session rather than per trial, as in the expert.
7-d.code_correctness_justification: video_offset() is called once in process_session and passed to every trajectory_signal call for both cameras; frame times come from the same trajectory_group the feature was read from, so a camera-specific frame count cannot desynchronise the two views. I verified the computed offsets match the values recorded in metadata['session_info'].

8-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Paw velocity* derived from?
8-a.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert: the bottom camera's 'top_paw' only. This respects the methods ('the paws were tracked using only the bottom view') and avoids 'bottom_paw', which the expert documents as dropping out through the delay epoch. The AI gives no reason for preferring top_paw, but it arrived at the same feature.
8-a.code_correctness_justification: find_feature_indices(h5, bottom, 'top_paw') resolves against the bottom camera's featNames, which I confirmed contains top_paw and bottom_paw; trajectory_signal is then called with the bottom group so both the ts array and the frameTimes come from that camera.

8-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Paw velocity*?
8-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same treatment as the tongue - interpolate, gradient, hypot, NaN preserved - and, like the expert, no normalisation since only one camera contributes, so values stay in pixel units. The AI departs from findVelocity.m in two places for non-tongue features: it does not subtract the baseline median derivative and does not nearest-fill the paw. Both departures are the right call for this task: nearest-filling would erase the 'not visible' class the decoder spec requires, and the expert makes the same two choices. Resulting not-visible fraction 14.5%, comparable to the expert's ~19%.
8-b.code_correctness_justification: The paw goes through the same trajectory_signal / speed_from_position path as the tongue with no special-casing, which is what the decision describes; the None-trial fallback produces a full 500-bin NaN trace.

8-c.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* thresholded into categories?
8-c.decision_correctness_justification: The same session-wide 50th-percentile split with a third 'not visible' class, matching the prompt and the expert.
8-c.code_correctness_justification: Same categorize_session_signal call; the output fractions (0.428/0.428/0.145) are an exact 50/50 split of the 85.5% visible bins, confirming a correct median threshold.

8-d.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* aligned with the neural data?
8-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the tongue and to the expert: the same per-session video offset, then subtraction of the trial's go cue, then interpolation onto the shared 10 ms grid - but using the bottom camera's own frameTimes, which is the same precaution the expert takes for the case where the two cameras record different frame counts.
8-d.code_correctness_justification: frameTimes is read from trajectory_group (the bottom group for the paw), not hard-coded to the side camera, and the same offset constant is applied.

9-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Motion energy* derived from?
9-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source as the expert: the standalone motionEnergy_<anm>_<date>.mat beside the data structure, one trace per trial with one value per side-camera frame, rather than the inconsistently present obj.me.
9-a.code_correctness_justification: load_motion_energy reads me['data'] and unwraps one further nested ['data'], mirroring loadMotionEnergy.m's 'if isstruct(me.data), me.data = me.data.data; end', and handles both the object-array and 2-D-matrix layouts with an explicit error otherwise. It would fail on the bare-cell-array layout the expert handles with a while loop, but the AI's cohort does not contain such a file (the script ran to completion on all 12).

9-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Motion energy*?
9-b.decision_correctness_justification: Like the expert, the AI recognises that the per-pixel median difference and 99th-percentile spatial reduction are already applied upstream and does nothing but resample. It differs in resampling by linear interpolation onto bin centres rather than bin-averaging, and in applying a nearest-fill afterwards - both of which are literally what loadMotionEnergy.m does (interp1 onto obj.time, then fillmissing(me.data, 'nearest')). The cost is that the fill extrapolates a constant into bins the camera never covered, which is why 'no video' ends up at only 0.03% of bins where the expert would leave them uncategorised; that is a deliberate inheritance of the source's behaviour rather than an oversight, though it does mean the third class is effectively unused for this output.
9-b.code_correctness_justification: nearest_fill correctly implements MATLAB's fillmissing 'nearest' semantics (searchsorted over the finite indices, tie broken toward the left as in MATLAB), and is applied only to motion energy, not to the tongue or paw. The <2-frame and no-finite-value guards produce all-NaN traces rather than garbage.

9-c.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* thresholded into categories?
9-c.decision_correctness_justification: Session-wide 50th percentile with a third class, as the prompt requires and the expert does. Correctly ignores the authors' manual per-session moveThresh stored in the motion-energy file, which the prompt's discretisation rule overrides.
9-c.code_correctness_justification: Same categorize_session_signal call; fractions 0.499/0.501/0.0003 are the expected near-exact median split.

9-d.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* aligned with the neural data?
9-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: motion energy has one value per side-camera frame, so it inherits the side camera's offset-corrected, go-cue-aligned frame times and is put on the same 10 ms grid. loadMotionEnergy.m likewise indexes obj.traj{1}(trix).frameTimes.
9-d.code_correctness_justification: The code literally reuses tongue[2], the aligned side-camera frame times already computed for the tongue, and truncates to min(len(me), len(frame_times)) so a length mismatch cannot misalign the trace. One coupling worth noting: if the side-camera trial was skipped by the NdroppedFrames guard, motion energy for that trial is dropped too, whereas loadMotionEnergy.m has a synthetic-frameTimes fallback; the affected trial count is negligible (no_video = 0.03% of bins).

10.question: How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?
10.decision_correctness_justification: Same philosophy as the expert: keep the trial, mark the gap, never interpolate over genuinely missing tracking. Trials with non-finite NdroppedFrames (the guard copied from findPosition.m), trials with fewer than two usable frame times, and frames where DeepLabCut failed all come out as 'not visible' rather than being filled or dropped; mismatched frame/coordinate/motion-energy lengths are handled by truncating to the common length, which is the same precaution the expert takes. Motion energy is the one stream that is nearest-filled, following the source. The one place the AI is more brittle than the expert is that a session with <2 trials or <10 curated units raises and aborts the entire conversion instead of being skipped - fine on this cohort, fragile if the cohort were widened.

11-c.decision_correctness_justification: The expert states that nothing is recomputed; the AI does repeat work.
